summary: A launch is a one-shot narrative event — distinct from a landing page (steady-state conversion), an exec memo (internal alignment), or a changelog (continuous release log).

facts.text: A launch is a one-shot narrative event - distinct from a landing page (steady-state conversion), an exec memo (internal alignment), or a changelog (continuous release log).
Heuristic: If you can't name the archetype in 10 seconds, the launch isn't ready.
Open with a one-paragraph claim about a shift in the world. Never open with the product. Andy Raskin's whole thesis: "the old game is over; a new game is starting."

facets.title: Beat 2 — Stakes (the cost of the old game)

facts.text: What does the reader lose by staying with the old way? Quantify if possible.
Now - and only now - name the product and the one-line description. Apple's pattern: "Today, Apple introduced [X], a [category] that [primary benefit]."
Customer logos, quotes, measurable outcomes, demo link. One outside voice is worth ten internal claims.

facets.title: Beat 5 — Call to action and honesty

facts.text: Clear CTA - one primary CTA, one secondary at most.
What's not in v1 - the honest-disclosure section.
A working "why now" paragraph:
Names a shift that has already occurred.
Establishes the cost of operating as if the shift hadn't happened.
Creates urgency that is "you're already behind if you ignore this."

Template: > Until recently, [old default] was the only way to [task]. But [shift A] and [shift B] have changed what's possible. Teams that adapt are [outcome]. Teams that don't are [cost]. Today we're announcing [product] to help you [verb] in this new world.
Anti-pattern: "AI is everywhere." This is a backdrop, not a why-now. It has no specific shift, no cost, no urgency.
Sequencing rules:
The blog post is the canonical source. Every other piece links to it.
Analyst and press briefings are under embargo.
Release notes accompany the announcement. When the blog post says "today we're launching X," the docs and the changelog must already reflect X.

facets.title: 5. The "what's not in v1" honesty section

facts.text: Template: > v1 deliberately ships without [X], [Y], and [Z]. We chose this scope to get [primary benefit] in your hands sooner. [X] is on the roadmap for [quarter]. If [X] or [Y] is a hard requirement for you today, [alternative path].
What this section does: Lets engineers in evaluation mode answer "can I use this yet?" without booking a call. Pre-empts the inevitable Hacker News commenter who finds the missing feature.
The "we're excited to announce" opener. Cut. Open with the shift.
The "this changes everything" overclaim.
The "product-first" structure. Specs, then features, then maybe a sentence about who cares.
The hidden "what's not in v1."
The "AI/cloud/edge is everywhere" why-now.
The post that doesn't match the docs.
The four-CTA ending. If you list four CTAs the reader picks zero.
Define before launch day. Sample tiers:
Unique pageviews on the blog post in week 1
Hacker News front page
Signups attributable to launch
New-product activation rate in week 1, week 4
Andy Raskin, "The Greatest Sales Deck I've Ever Seen" (Medium / Mission.org, 2016)
Apple Newsroom (apple.com/newsroom)
Linear changelog (linear.app/changelog)
Stripe Blog launches (stripe.com/blog)
Lenny Rachitsky, lennysnewsletter.com
Announcing a new product or major feature where the writer needs to justify why now, rather than just listing what shipped.

facts.text: A launch narrative works best as a one-shot event — reusing launch-style beats for routine, continuous updates that belong in a changelog dilutes both the launch's impact and the changelog's usefulness.
